questions.q: Where do the driver's button and stick inputs show up?
questions.explain: gamepad1 is where all of driver one's stick and button inputs appear. You read fields like gamepad1.left_stick_y and gamepad1.a from it.

questions.q: What type holds a joystick axis value?
questions.correct: A double, because axes have decimals
wrong: An int, because axes are always whole
A boolean, because axes are on or off
A String, because axes are made of text
questions.explain: Stick axes are smooth values from -1.0 to 1.0, so they use double (which holds decimals). Buttons, being on/off, use boolean instead.

questions.q: What is the range of a joystick axis?
questions.explain: Each stick axis runs from -1.0 to 1.0. A gentle push might read 0.2; letting go returns it to 0.0.

questions.q: What type holds a button's value?
questions.correct: A boolean, either true or false
wrong: A double, with many decimal places
An int, a plain whole-number count
A String, made out of letters
questions.explain: A button is either pressed or not, so it uses boolean — true when held, false when released. gamepad1.a is a boolean.

questions.q: When you push a stick UP, the Y value reads...
questions.correct: Negative, which is how the hardware reports it
wrong: Positive, the same as pushing it down
Zero, until you push it much harder
Exactly 1.0, no matter how far you push
questions.explain: Pushing up gives a NEGATIVE y value — that's just how the hardware reports it. You flip the sign with -gamepad1.left_stick_y so that up means forward.

questions.q: Which reads the left stick's up-and-down position?
questions.explain: left_stick_y is the left stick's up/down axis; left_stick_x is its left/right axis. Y is vertical, X is horizontal.

questions.q: Which reads the A face button?
questions.explain: The face buttons are gamepad1.a, gamepad1.b, gamepad1.x, and gamepad1.y — each a boolean that's true while held.

questions.q: Why must you flip the sign of left_stick_y for forward driving?
questions.correct: Because pushing up reads as a negative value
wrong: Because pushing up reads as a huge value
Because the stick only reports whole numbers
Because the battery reverses the raw signal
questions.explain: Up on the stick is negative, but you want up to mean "drive forward" (positive). So you write -gamepad1.left_stick_y to flip it.

questions.q: A gentle push on a stick gives a value like...
questions.explain: Stick axes are proportional — a light push might read 0.2, a hard push nears 1.0. That lets you drive gently or quickly.

questions.correct: The farther you push, the faster it goes
wrong: The stick has only fully on or off
The value is always exactly one
Every button does the same thing
questions.explain: Proportional means the output scales with the push. Push the stick a little and the wheels turn slowly; push it all the way and they go full speed.

questions.q: Which axis is left-and-right on a stick?
questions.explain: X is the left/right (horizontal) axis; Y is the up/down (vertical) axis. So left_stick_x is left/right and left_stick_y is up/down.

questions.correct: true while B is held, false otherwise
wrong: The number of times B was pressed
The letter B stored as plain text
questions.explain: gamepad1.b is a boolean — true while the B button is held down and false when it's released.

questions.q: Releasing a stick returns its axis to...
questions.explain: When you let go, the stick recenters and its axis reads 0.0 — no push, no output.

questions.q: To store a stick value, the variable type should be...
questions.explain: A stick axis is a decimal, so store it in a double. A button, being true/false, would use a boolean.

questions.q: Why does the same stick feel different in two programs?
questions.correct: The code decides what each input actually does
wrong: The stick quietly rewires its own hardware
The battery picks the behavior each time
The referee sets it before every match
questions.explain: The gamepad just reports numbers; your code decides what they do. So the same stick can drive, aim, or lift depending on the program.
